vignette:
Sione presents as a man meticulously put together, his clothes pressed, his silver hair neatly combed. At 74, he carries the quiet dignity of a Samoan elder, though his eyes, magnified slightly by his reading glasses, hold a deep and unsettled weariness. He is an editor, a man who has spent forty years imposing order on the chaos of language, yet he speaks of his own life with a hesitant, fragmented narrative he cannot seem to correct.

His story begins not in his youth, but just six years ago. After a quiet divorce decades earlier and years of comfortable solitude, he met Elena. She was vibrant, ten years his junior, and filled his quiet apartment with a life he hadn’t realized he was missing. For the first year, it was a late-in-life renaissance. They traveled, hosted dinners, and he felt a warmth he thought was reserved for younger men. He speaks of this time with a kind of pained nostalgia, as if describing a beautiful, intricate story he once edited, knowing the tragic ending that awaits the final pages.

The change was gradual, a series of subtle edits to their life together. It began with sharp words, criticisms that cut deeper than he let on. He, a man raised to be a protector, a steady presence, found himself constantly off-balance. He started to second-guess his words, his actions, his very thoughts, trying to smooth over the narrative and restore the peace. He attributes this to his own failings. “I am not an easy man,” he says, looking at his hands. “Too quiet. Too set in my ways.”

The first time she threw something, it was a teacup, a delicate porcelain thing he’d inherited from his mother. It shattered against the wall behind his head. The shock was absolute. He remembers the sound more than anything—the sharp crack that bifurcated his life into a “before” and an “after.” He remembers kneeling to pick up the pieces, the gritty feel of sugar and ceramic under his palm, and the overwhelming, suffocating shame. He told no one. How could he explain that this woman, who he loved, had done this? And that he, a man of his size and standing, had simply knelt and cleaned it up?

The violence escalated over the next two years. It was never predictable. It would erupt from moments of placid domesticity—a disagreement over a news article, a burnt piece of toast. He learned to read the subtle shifts in her tone, the tightening of her jaw, the way her eyes would go flat. He became a master of de-escalation, his body in a constant state of high alert, braced for an impact he could never quite anticipate. His large frame, once a source of pride, felt like a liability, a clumsy prop in a play where he had forgotten all his lines.

He finally left after she threw a heavy glass paperweight during an argument, missing his face by inches. He packed a single bag while she was out and never returned. That was three years ago. But he never truly left.

Now, his world has shrunk to the size of his apartment. His work, once a refuge, is a struggle. He finds himself re-reading the same paragraph a dozen times, the words blurring into meaningless shapes. Any sudden noise from the street below—a car backfiring, a shout—sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. He keeps the chain on his door at all times.

He avoids his family, declining invitations for birthdays and holidays. The shame is a physical weight, a constant companion. He feels he has brought dishonor to his name, that he is a fraud. He has nightmares most nights, waking up in a cold sweat with the scent of her perfume thick in the air and the echo of her voice in his ears. During the day, he is haunted by intrusive images: the spray of tea against the wallpaper, the glint of light on the glass paperweight as it flew past his head. He feels profoundly disconnected from the man he once was—the calm, respected editor, the proud father, the dignified Samoan man. He is now just the custodian of a story he cannot bear to read, but one from which he can never look away.
